concepts.name: Trusted proxy handling of forwarded headers
Re-reading request bodies with bounded buffering

questions.prompt: TLS terminates at a trusted proxy, which forwards HTTP to ASP.NET Core. HTTPS redirection loops because the app sees HTTP. Which setup addresses the underlying cause?

choices.text: Trust all incoming X-Forwarded-Proto values from direct public clients
Set every request scheme to HTTPS without checking its origin
Run HTTPS redirection before processing any forwarded headers
Process configured trusted forwarded headers before redirection

questions.explanation: Trusted forwarded headers restore the original HTTPS scheme before HTTPS redirection runs. Blindly trusting public headers permits spoofing, and late middleware cannot fix the redirect decision.

sources.title: Configure ASP.NET Core for proxy servers
sources.claim: Forwarded headers restore scheme and client information behind trusted proxies; known proxy/network restrictions limit spoofing and middleware must precede HTTPS redirection.

questions.prompt: A cookie-authenticated ASP.NET Core API configures `AllowAnyOrigin().AllowCredentials()`. What is wrong with this CORS policy?

choices.text: Credentials are sent only after the server removes every cookie
It combines credentials with an insecure unrestricted origin
AllowAnyOrigin validates each origin against the user's role
The wildcard forces all cross-origin requests to become anonymous

questions.explanation: An unrestricted origin plus credentials is insecure; ASP.NET Core returns an invalid CORS response for that combination. Use a narrow trusted-origin policy rather than treating CORS as user authorization.

sources.title: Enable Cross-Origin Requests in ASP.NET Core
sources.claim: AllowAnyOrigin combined with AllowCredentials is insecure and yields an invalid CORS response; credentialed access should allow trusted explicit origins.

questions.prompt: Middleware enables ASP.NET Core request-body buffering before reading a large body. Which statements hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Every buffered body remains entirely in managed memory
Bodies above the configured threshold can spill to disk
A configured buffering limit can cause IOException when exceeded
The threshold rejects any request larger than the memory buffer
Buffering can make the request body readable more than once

questions.explanation: EnableBuffering supports repeated reads. The threshold controls memory versus disk, not a hard rejection size. A separate buffer limit can throw IOException when the body exceeds it.

sources.title: HttpRequestRewindExtensions.EnableBuffering
sources.claim: EnableBuffering allows repeated body reads, spills beyond a memory threshold to disk, and a configured limit causes IOException when exceeded.

questions.prompt: A public client supplies a forged X-Forwarded-For header directly to an ASP.NET Core server. Why configure known proxy addresses instead of trusting every sender?

choices.text: To accept forwarded identity only through trusted hops
To encrypt the forwarded client IP using the proxy certificate
To prove the remote client owns the IP stated in its header
To use a forwarded client IP as proof that the client is authenticated

questions.explanation: Known proxy/network restrictions ensure only trusted forwarders supply that metadata. A header alone proves neither ownership nor authenticity and is not encrypted by this configuration.

sources.title: Configure ASP.NET Core for proxy servers
sources.claim: Forwarded headers restore scheme and client information behind trusted proxies; known proxy/network restrictions limit spoofing and middleware must precede HTTPS redirection.

questions.prompt: A browser SPA at https://portal.example needs credentialed access to its API. Which CORS origin setup fits this requirement?

choices.text: Allow every origin and reflect its value while enabling browser credentials
Return a wildcard origin together with permission for cookies
Allow the trusted portal origin explicitly and allow credentials
Remove CORS entirely and rely on the cookie's encryption alone

questions.explanation: Credentialed cross-origin access needs an explicitly permitted trusted origin. A wildcard does not grant valid credentialed browser access, and cookie encryption does not replace the browser's CORS checks.

sources.title: Enable Cross-Origin Requests in ASP.NET Core
sources.claim: AllowAnyOrigin combined with AllowCredentials is insecure and yields an invalid CORS response; credentialed access should allow trusted explicit origins.

questions.prompt: A service sets both a memory threshold and a total limit with `EnableBuffering`. Which conclusions are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Reading past the total limit continues automatically using disk storage
Crossing the memory threshold need not reject the request
The total limit automatically raises the threshold to the body size
The buffering strategy can use temporary disk storage
Buffering guarantees that arbitrarily large bodies can be accepted

questions.explanation: The threshold changes storage strategy, while the limit bounds accepted buffered data. Temporary files can hold larger bodies, but exceeding the separate total limit may throw; buffering is not unlimited.

sources.title: HttpRequestRewindExtensions.EnableBuffering
sources.claim: EnableBuffering allows repeated body reads, spills beyond a memory threshold to disk, and a configured limit causes IOException when exceeded.
